newsitem.title: USA: Higher Aug NAPM more evidence for Fed - US experts.
newsitem.headline: Higher Aug NAPM more evidence for Fed - US experts.

text.p: A rebound in the U.S. manufacturing sector in August marks yet another sign of a strengthening economy which may soon tilt the scales toward a Federal Reserve tightening of credit policy, economists said.

"All the latest numbers point towards a strengthening U.S. economy," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc. "The third quarter started with a whimper, but it looks like it's going to end with a bang in terms of the economic outlook. It looks like the Fed will have to tighten at the September 24 meeting if not before," he added.
Jones said forecasters should not rule out the prospects for a between-policy-meetings Fed tightening sometime after crucial August jobs data are released on Friday, September 6.
Earlier Tuesday, the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) reported a rise to 52.6 in its August index of business conditions versus a reading of 50.2 in July.
After tumbling four points to a reading of 50.2 in July, economists had predicted a rebound to 52.9 last month following last Friday's strong jump in a regional report.
The Chicago association of purchasing managers' survey printed 60.0 in August versus 51.2 in July.

Experts agree the latest NAPM report is consistent with a stronger manufacturing sector. And other reports such as those on new home sales and auto sales further support the idea of a bouyant economy.
Prior to the NAPM release, market observers were zeroed in on the employment component of the manufacturing report to shed some light on Friday's August employment data.
The NAPM employment index came in at 48.2 up from 45.5.

"The employment component fits with a 200,000 payroll employment increase, but it doesn't give a strong signal that the payrolls number will be higher than that," said Elliot Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin, and Jenrette Securities Corp.
In a Reuter poll, U.S. economists expect a 244,000 increase in payrolls for August and expect the unemployment rate to dip to 5.3 percent.
"From the Federal Reserve's standpoint, we are still very very contingent on Friday's (employment) numbers. I think it's a very tough call," Platt said.
He predicted that if payrolls grow by 200,000 or less, the Fed will keep monetary policy unchanged.
The next meeting of the central bank's policy-setting Federal Reserve Open Market Committee is scheduled for September 24.
